title: Mary Anning, fossil hunter
keyIdea: Mary Anning (1799–1847) hunted fossils on the beach below the cliffs at Lyme Regis, in Dorset, England. Winter storms brought rock down and washed fossils out, so she searched after storms, even though falling rock was dangerous. In 1811 her brother Joseph found a long skull, and about a year later Mary, aged about 12, dug out the rest: an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile with paddles and a tail fin. In 1823 she found the first whole plesiosaur, and in 1828 a pterosaur, a flying reptile. None of these were dinosaurs, and the word 'dinosaur' was not made up until 1842. Her fossils were of animals that are no longer alive, which helped scientists accept that animals can become extinct. Women could not join the Geological Society, so men often wrote about her finds without her name.
familyTip: Look up the Lyme Regis cliffs on a map together, then find a picture of Mary's ichthyosaur at the Natural History Museum. Ask: 'Which animal alive today does it look like, and why is it not that animal?' If you ever hunt for fossils on a beach, go at low tide with a grown-up, after a storm, and keep away from the foot of the cliff.

visual.caption: A dinosaur, or one of Mary's reptiles that was not a dinosaur? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: storm the cliff to find fossils, build the ichthyosaur, sort dinosaurs from sea reptiles, order her finds, match look-alikes.

kid: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a town by the sea in England. Her family was poor. Mary and her brother Joseph sold fossils to help pay for food.

The cliffs at Lyme Regis are full of fossils. In winter, big storms make the rock fall. The sea washes the stones. Then the fossils show. Mary went out after storms. It was risky. Rock could fall on her.

In 1811 Joseph found a long skull with sharp teeth. A year later, Mary dug out the rest. It was a sea reptile called an ichthyosaur. It had a long snout, a backbone, four paddles and a tail fin. Later she found a plesiosaur, with a long neck, and a pterosaur, which could fly.

These were not dinosaurs. They were reptiles of the sea and the air. No animal like them is alive now. They are extinct. Mary's finds helped show that animals can die out for good. In her time, women could not join the science club for rocks. Men wrote about her fossils, and they often left out her name. Now she is famous.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. Mary Anning (1799–1847) is a common choice of a key person from the past in the KS1 history curriculum in England. Her finds also back up KS2 science on fossils and how life has changed. Key words: fossil, ichthyosaur (a sea reptile), plesiosaur (a sea reptile with a long neck), pterosaur (a flying reptile), extinct.

The cliffs at Lyme Regis are made of rock called Blue Lias. It is about 200 million years old. Winter storms and landslips bring down fresh rock full of fossils, so hunters go out after storms. That is also why the cliffs are unsafe: a landslip killed Mary's dog, Tray, in 1833. Joseph found the skull in 1811 and Mary dug out the body in 1812. It is now in the Natural History Museum in London. In 1823 she found the first whole plesiosaur. A top French expert, Georges Cuvier, first thought it was a fake. In 1828 she found the first pterosaur known outside Germany.

Common mistakes: calling ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pterosaurs dinosaurs. They are other groups of reptiles, and the name dinosaur was made up by Richard Owen in 1842. Some children think the skull was a crocodile, as some people did at first. Some think a look-alike that lives now, such as a dolphin, means the animal is not extinct. And some think she was welcomed by the experts of her day. Women could not join the Geological Society of London until 1919, and her name was often left out when her fossils were written up. In 2010 the Royal Society named her one of ten British women who did most for science.

In the lab your child sees that fossils turn up only after a storm brings rock down. They pick out fossils by shape and rebuild the ichthyosaur, turning down legs and wings. They sort dinosaurs from Mary's reptiles and put six dates in order, to see that the word dinosaur came 30 years after her first big find. Last, they match each fossil to a look-alike that lives today, to see that it is extinct.

practice.prompt: Where did Mary Anning find her fossils?
choices: On the beach below the cliffs at Lyme Regis
In the sand of a desert
practice.hint: Mary lived in a small town by the sea, in Dorset.
practice.explain: She searched the beach below the Lyme Regis cliffs, where storms brought fossil-filled rock down.

practice.prompt: What kind of animal was Mary's ichthyosaur?
practice.hint: Think about its paddles, and the group dinosaurs belong to.
practice.explain: An ichthyosaur was a sea reptile with paddles and a tail fin. It was not a dinosaur, and not a fish.

practice.prompt: Mary found her ichthyosaur in 1812. The word 'dinosaur' was made up in 1842. How many years later was that?
practice.hint: Take 1812 away from 1842. Count on from 1812 in tens.
practice.explain: 1842 − 1812 = 30 years. So Mary could not have called her finds dinosaurs.

practice.prompt: Mary was born in 1799. How old would she be in {y}? (Work it out as {y} take away 1799.)
practice.hint: Take 1799 away from the year. Counting on from 1799 to 1800 is 1.
practice.explain: {y} − 1799 = {=y-1799}. Mary did most of her hunting as a child and a young woman.

practice.prompt: An ichthyosaur has 4 paddles. Mary finds {n} whole ichthyosaurs. How many paddles is that?
practice.hint: Each ichthyosaur has 4 paddles. Count in fours.

pool.prompt: When is the best time to look for fossils at Lyme Regis?
choices: After a winter storm, with a grown-up, away from the cliff
On a calm day, digging into the cliff
At high tide, at the foot of the cliff
pool.hint: What brings the rock down, and what keeps you safe?
pool.explain: Storms bring rock down and wash fossils out. Stay away from the cliff and the tide, and go with a grown-up.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a dinosaur?
pool.explain: Iguanodon walked on land, so it is a dinosaur. A plesiosaur swam and a pterosaur flew: both were other reptiles.

pool.prompt: Joseph found a long skull with sharp teeth. Some people thought it was a crocodile. What was it?
pool.hint: Mary found the body. It had paddles and a tail fin.
pool.explain: The body Mary dug out had paddles and a tail fin, so it was an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile.

pool.prompt: An ichthyosaur looks like a dolphin. Are ichthyosaurs alive today?
pool.hint: Looking alike is not the same as being the same animal.
pool.explain: No ichthyosaur is alive today. A dolphin is a mammal. It only looks like one.

pool.prompt: Why did men often write about Mary's fossils without her name?
choices: Women could not join the science societies then
pool.hint: Who was allowed into the Geological Society?
pool.explain: Only men could join the Geological Society then, so Mary's name was often left out.

choices: They showed animals that are now extinct once lived
pool.hint: Is any animal like an ichthyosaur alive now?
pool.explain: Her fossils were of animals that no longer live, which helped scientists accept that animals can die out.

pool.prompt: Mary finds {a} ammonites and {b} belemnites on the beach. How many fossils is that?
pool.hint: Add the two kinds of fossil together.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} fossils. She sold small fossils like these to visitors.

pool.prompt: Mary found a fossil in {y}. The word 'dinosaur' was made up in 1842. How many years before 1842 was her find?
pool.hint: Take the year of the find away from 1842.
pool.explain: 1842 − {y} = {=1842-y} years. Mary's big finds all came before anyone said 'dinosaur'.
